source.title: Small Language Models Are Good Too: An Empirical Study of Zero-Shot Classification
source.authors: Pierre Lepagnol; Thomas Gerald; Sahar Ghannay; Christophe Servan; Sophie Rosset

record.file_problem: Minor PDF extraction and formatting artifacts; the full paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests model-size associations with downstream zero-shot classification performance, but uses accuracy/F1 correlations rather than the original studies’ held-out pretraining-loss scaling measurements.
record.gate_note: The study reports correlations between parameter count and downstream classification Acc/F1, and architecture comparisons on Acc/F1. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy, sweep training tokens or compute, fit power laws, or evaluate compute-optimal allocations. Architecture-comparison rows are recorded under fits_no_version because they use downstream Acc/F1 rather than loss.
record.test_reason: The study correlates parameter count (77M–40B, 72 models) with zero-shot classification Acc/F1 on 15 datasets. Its stated aim and result is that bigger is not consistently better. That bears directly on V6, read as 'downstream performance improves with scale'. Size is pooled across heterogeneous model families, training data and instruction tuning, so it is not a controlled within-family scaling sweep. No loss is measured, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that small models (77M–3B) can match or surpass larger ones in zero-shot classification. They find larger size does not consistently improve performance across datasets, architecture matters on specific datasets, and instruction tuning helps in a dataset- and architecture-dependent way (significant for encoder-decoder only). Scoring function choice makes no significant difference.
record.recipe_differences: Compares downstream zero-shot classification Acc/F1 across pretrained models and parameter counts; it does not reproduce held-out cross-entropy scaling-law measurements or compute-optimal training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported model-size association varies by dataset and architecture. The authors also report dataset-dependent architecture effects on downstream Acc/F1.

fits_no_version.finding: After controlling for log parameter count, architecture (encoder-decoder vs decoder-only) significantly affects zero-shot Acc/F1 on 7 of 15 datasets (ANCOVA p<0.05); imdb is borderline.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture family affects zero-shot classification Acc/F1 at matched size on some datasets. This is downstream accuracy, not held-out loss, so it is not a V4 test.

fits_no_version.finding: Architecture effect on Acc/F1 is not significant for cdr, ethos, financial_phrasebank, sst-2, sst-5, trec and yelp.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture effects on zero-shot Acc/F1 are dataset-dependent; not a loss-based test of V4.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Language Resources and Evaluation
record.problems: The paper's prose says 10 of 15 datasets have p-values above 0.05 for the size relationship, but Table 3 appears to show 12 above 0.05. The study uses downstream classification scores rather than pretraining loss, and its prompts are hand-crafted with one prompt per dataset. It notes that pretraining time, data quality, dataset biases, statistical-tool choices, and omitted models may affect generalizability.
record.rows_left_out: No separately reported rows from the size-correlation or architecture-ANCOVA tables were omitted. Other instruction-tuning and scoring-function analyses were not included because they do not test the claim versions’ scaling, loss, or downstream size-predictability measures.

untested.parts: Downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss; controlled within-family scaling (same data and recipe, varying size); quantitative forecasting of downstream scores from small models.

record.verdict_notes: Main caveat: model size is pooled across many families (BLOOM, Pythia, Falcon, LaMini, T5, mT0, etc.) with different data and instruction tuning, so the correlations confound size with recipe. They do not measure scaling within a family. Data points appear to pool models with scoring functions (appendix says scores were averaged), so the sample basis is unclear. The record's 'problems' field misreads the prose: '10 of 15 above 0.05' plus 'agnews and chemprot near threshold' sums to the 12 non-significant datasets in Table 3, so prose and table are consistent. Single hand-crafted prompt per dataset.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law relationship in parameters, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run fits or extrapolations to larger runs are reported.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and tokens is tested.
Architecture is compared using downstream Acc/F1, not held-out loss; there is no direct fixed-parameter comparison of loss across depth, width, or other architecture details.
The study concerns text classification with pretrained language models and does not test whether a loss power law holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests associations of parameter count with downstream Acc/F1; does not test downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss or establish predictive forecasts.
Does not fit scaling-law exponents or compare fitting choices, training schedules, data choices, or curve bending.

relationships.condition: cdr dataset, size pooled across all models
relationships.reason: Significant positive size–Acc/F1 correlation (r=0.25, p=0.0002; d03).
relationships.display_finding: Model size has a significant positive correlation with accuracy and F1, with r = 0.25 and p = 0.0002.

relationships.reason: Only a weak, borderline positive correlation (r=0.13, p=0.053; d04).
relationships.display_finding: The positive correlation was weak and borderline, with r=0.13 and p=0.053.

relationships.condition: ethos and imdb datasets; decoder-only models pooled across datasets
relationships.reason: Significant negative size–performance correlations: ethos r=-0.15 (d05), imdb r=-0.29 (d07), decoder r=-0.04 (d16). This is across heterogeneous families, not within-family scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Size–performance correlations were significantly negative for ethos, r=−0.15, imdb, r=−0.29, and pooled decoder-only models, r=−0.04, across heterogeneous model families.

relationships.condition: agnews, bbcnews, financial_phrasebank, semeval, sms, spouse, sst-2, sst-5, trec, yelp, youtube; encoder-decoder models pooled
relationships.reason: No significant size–Acc/F1 association (all p>0.05; |r|≤0.14) in rows d01, d02, d06, d08–d15, d17. This holds with size confounded by model family.
relationships.display_finding: No significant size–accuracy or size–F1 association appeared for agnews, bbcnews, financial_phrasebank, semeval, sms, spouse, sst-2, sst-5, trec, yelp, youtube or pooled encoder-decoder models, with all p>0.05 and |r|≤0.14, while model family remained confounded with size.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The reported size–Acc/F1 correlation is positive and significant (row d03), though this is an association rather than a demonstrated forecast.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: ethos and imdb datasets; decoder-only aggregate
reader_labels.reason: Significant negative size–performance correlations run opposite to expected improvement with scale (rows d05, d07, d16).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Datasets with reported non-significant size associations, excluding the near-threshold agnews and chemprot results; encoder-decoder aggregate
reader_labels.reason: The table reports no significant association for these dataset conditions and for the encoder-decoder aggregate (rows d02, d06, d08-d13, d15, d17).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The reported p-values are just above 0.05 and the paper describes the correlations as inconclusive, limiting conclusions for these settings (rows d01, d04).
